newsitem.title: UK: US stocks in London steady, await FOMC decision.
newsitem.headline: US stocks in London steady, await FOMC decision.

text.p: U.S. shares were steady in quiet trade on Tuesday following Wall Street's 100-point late surge Monday but European investors remained cautious, fearing that the Dow's advance may be short-lived.
"There just wasn't much meat in the Dow's rally yesterday," said Kirit Shah, strategist at Sanwa International.
"I think what we saw was some short-covering ahead of the FOMC meeting. I can't see the Dow being able to sustain any move above the 7,000 level."
U.S. blue chips jumped sharply on Monday as investors bet the market had already prepared itself for a 25 basis point Fed rate hike after Tuesday's FOMC monetary policy meeting.

The Dow Industrials finished 100.46 points up at 6,905.25. But, in the broader market, decliners outpaced advancing issues by 1,322 to 1,170. The tech-laden Nasdaq Composite continued its decline, losing 11.43 points to 1,242.64.

The Nasdaq Composite has underperformed the Dow by around 10 percent over the past three months, according to data from Reuters Securities 3000. Shah points to Nasdaq's recent weakness as evidence the U.S. share market has entered a bear phase. He expects volatility to increase on Wall Street culminating in a gradual drift towards the 6,300 level.
"I don't think we will see any dramatic downturn, just a slow move downwards," Shah said.
Chris Chaitow, technical analyst at Robert Fleming, also thinks the Dow is headed into a bear market but does not rule out a re-test of its record high of 7,112.10, set on March 11.
"Volatility will increase giving a lot of confusing signals over the next couple of months," Chaitow said. "Then when everyone is totally confused, the market will head downwards."
In the near-term, Chaitow said the Dow had to close above the 6,950 level if it was to challenge its record highs.
Only a handful of issues traded in London by 1110 GMT.
Motorola was up $3/8 to $57-3/4 after the Wall Street Journal reported that the company was on the verge of winning a "potentially significant" digital cellular telephone contract in Japan.
GM added $1/8 to $58 after the company signed a long-awaited $1.57 billion joint venture to produce medium-sized cars in China.
Boeing, which also signed a $685 million contract on Tuesday to sell jets to China, was up $3/8 to $106-1/8.

Elsewhere, Philip Morris, which rose $4-3/8 in New York on Monday, was up $1/4 to $116-1/8 despite news that James Kilts, executive vice president of the company's worldwide foods division had resigned.
Kilts led a two-year turnaround at the company's Kraft Foods unit, according to a report in the Wall Street Journal.
"European investors haven't really taken notice of the resignation. I suspect the news will have a bigger impact in the U.S. later today," one market maker said.
The June T-bond was up 8/32 to 109-7/32 while the yield on the cash 30-year long bond stood at 6.92 percent.
The June S&P 500 futures contract was down 1.20 points to 800.05.
--Dale Faulken, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
